# Imaging Diagnosis: Imaging Diagnosis of Lateral Plantar Digital Vein Thrombosis in a Yearling Thoroughbred

**Authors:** Miriam R Garcia‐Collao; Jorge L Sanclemente; Diego S Larriva; Gregory D Roberts; Claude A Ragle

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Veterinary Clinical Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine, Washington State University, Pullman, Washington, USA

## Abstract

A 1‐year‐old thoroughbred filly was referred to the Washington State Veterinary Teaching Hospital with a 4‐month history of left hind limb swelling, from the mid metatarsus to the distal pastern, without lameness. Previous imaging (digital radiographs, ultrasound, and low‐field magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) was inconclusive, with a tentative diagnosis of lymphatic drainage impairment. A high‐field MRI diagnosed left lateral plantar digital vein thrombosis, with secondary lymphatic dilation and edema. The filly was discharged with rehabilitation instructions and resumed exercise shortly after. No lameness was observed, and swelling significantly decreased over time. This case highlights the benefit of magnetic resonance in diagnosing previously unreported equine vascular conditions.

Keywords: edema, horse, magnetic resonance, thrombosis

magnetic resonance imaging

plantar vein thrombosis

## Signalment, History, and Clinical Findings

A 1‐year‐old Thoroughbred filly (380 kg) was admitted to the Washington State Veterinary Teaching Hospital for a left hind distal limb swelling that had persisted for 4 months with no lameness observed. Left hind fetlock digital radiographs and ultrasonography, as well as low‐field magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (unavailable for review) performed by the referring veterinarian 3 months prior to presentation, did not yield a definitive diagnosis. The condition was initially suspected to be a puncture wound and was treated medically by the referring veterinarian with a 10‐day course of systemic antimicrobial therapy consisting of sulfamethoxazole–trimethoprim. Despite exercise recommendations due to a suspected lymphatic drainage impairment, the swelling continued to worsen. As this yearling was intended to become a racehorse, the owner´s concern was that it would be rejected during a pre‐race veterinary inspection.

On presentation, the filly was alert and bright, with a body temperature of 100.8°F, a respiratory rate of 30 breaths/min, and a heart rate of 40 bpm. Mild‐to‐moderate swelling was observed around the left hind fetlock, extending from mid metatarsus to the distal pastern. On palpation, the edema was identified as diffuse, soft, and fluid‐filled with pitting edema. No wounds were observed. Owing to the filly's young age and absence of prior training, the lameness evaluation was limited to straight‐line assessment on an asphalt surface using an equine gait analysis system (Equinosis Q), which revealed no evidence of lameness.

A lymphatic or venous drainage abnormality was suspected on the basis of clinical assessment, given the chronic history described and the absence of additional abnormal findings at presentation, and further diagnostics with advanced imaging techniques were recommended. A complete physical examination and bloodwork revealed no significant abnormalities and indicated that the yearling was a good candidate for general anesthesia.

## Imaging, Diagnosis, and Outcome

A bilateral hind fetlock MRI was performed under general anesthesia using a 3‐T scanner (3.0‐Tesla Philips Ingenia) to enable a detailed evaluation of the affected area and comparative analysis with the contralateral limb. The horse was induced into general anesthesia using ketamine and midazolam and maintained under general anesthesia with inhaled isoflurane. The horse was positioned in left lateral recumbency for the bilateral study, during which scanning was performed from the mid‐cannon bone to the mid‐distal phalanx. The total study duration was 47 min and 23 s. The MRI findings on the yearling showed a moderate circumferential thickening of the subcutaneous tissues of the left limb, extending from the distal metatarsus through to the hoof capsule, predominantly T2 hyperintense (edema). The lateral plantar vein proximal to the pastern joint exhibited predominantly hyperintense signal on all sequences, with focal central hypointensity, comprising approximately 40% of the luminal area, most pronounced proximally and consistent with residual thrombus. The remaining lumen demonstrated a hyperintense signal compatible with partial recanalization. A large increase in the number of distended, tubular, T2‐hyperintense structures just palmar to the third metatarsal bone in the left limb was observed, presumed to represent either distended lymphatics or collateral venous distension, as definitive differentiation is not possible on non‐contrast MRI. Focal compression of the plantar lateral digital artery at the level of the sesamoid bone was observed bilaterally, likely secondary to an external positioning device, as suggested by the distortion of the cutaneous margin. This finding is consistent with a positioning‐related imaging artifact rather than true vascular pathology. Osseous, ligamentous, and tendinous structures of both limbs were normal.

The final established diagnosis was left lateral plantar digital vein thrombosis, accompanied by secondary lymphatic dilation and limb edema. Notably, partial recanalization of the affected vein was suggested.

The yearling was discharged from the hospital with a recommendation for a gradual return to exercise, along with manipulative therapy consisting of regular manual lymphatic drainage massage. This therapy involved rhythmic strokes and pumping motions applied manually, performed three times per week, with the aim of promoting edema reduction and minimizing the risk of fibrosis formation. Clinical follow‐up at 7 months confirmed the full resumption of training activities aimed at racing for 2 months without lameness or recurrence of excessive swelling.

## Discussion

On the basis of a literature search, the thrombosis of the lateral plantar digital vein, accompanied by secondary venous dilation and limb edema, has not been previously reported in horses. In this case, magnetic resonance proved to be a valuable tool for accurately characterizing the condition. Various etiologies have been identified in human literature, including increased mechanical load or stress, which can induce repeated microtrauma to the veins and trigger the activation of the coagulation cascade. Additional contributing factors include altered venous return, endothelial injury, and, in some cases, idiopathic causes [1, 2, 3]. These mechanisms can be understood within the framework of Virchow's triad (stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability) [1]. In the present case, the suspected puncture wound likely represents the primary factor, although the potential roles of stasis and hypercoagulability cannot be excluded.

Lateral plantar veins are reported to be more commonly affected than medial veins in humans [1], an observation mirrored in the present equine case. In humans, this distribution has been attributed to anatomical differences, including a slightly larger caliber of the lateral digital veins, and a more muscular venous course [4]. In horses, no anatomical size variations between medial and lateral veins have been described [5]. However, the medial structures are located deeper, potentially rendering the lateral side more exposed to trauma and therefore more susceptible to endothelial injury and subsequent thrombosis.

In the present study, a penetrating wound was initially suspected and treated with systemic antibiotics. However, there was no improvement, and the horse experienced progressive swelling in the leg over several months, which affected its physical appearance and could pose a potential issue during veterinary inspections at the racetracks. In equine practice, the opportunity to perform advanced imaging on horses presenting mild clinical signs is uncommon, as many cases do not warrant such in‐depth diagnostic procedures. However, the owner's concern regarding potential racetrack rejection, along with the pursuit of a definitive diagnosis, provided a unique opportunity to conduct more advanced imaging.

The most likely origin of the condition in this case is associated with the described traumatic event, which led to a vascular and lymphatic anomaly. This region of the limb serves as an important vascular pump; consequently, the impairment reduced the efficiency of blood return from the leg to the heart, contributing to the development of tissue edema. In humans, this pathology has been identified as a cause of foot pain, with clinical signs, including unilateral swelling, edema, pain, and a sensation of “heaviness or fullness” [1, 3, 6]. The time from onset to diagnosis can take up to 4 weeks, which may account for the more extensive involvement observed in some cases [1, 4, 7]. This presentation can be extrapolated to this particular case, as unilateral swelling over the last 4 months was present with no lameness signs.

Doppler ultrasound has traditionally been considered the gold standard for diagnosing thrombosis in humans [8]. Nonetheless, MRI is increasingly important due to its ability to rule out other differential diagnoses of foot pain, such as plantar fasciitis, tendinous involvement, bursitis, Morton's neuroma, stress fractures, sesamoiditis, and ganglion cysts [1, 4, 9]. In equines, the ultrasonography of the distal limb is routinely performed to evaluate injuries of tendons, tendon sheaths, and ligaments. Moreover, its use has been described for identifying vascular compromise following contrast administration [10]. Doppler ultrasonography is recommended for evaluating suspected vascular disease in equine limbs and is convenient for follow‐up of lesions [10, 11, 12]. In this case, ultrasonography performed by the referring veterinarian did not yield a definitive diagnosis and was not repeated at our institution, as MRI was considered the preferred diagnostic modality based on the differential list. The absence of a dedicated ultrasound evaluation at our institution represents a limitation of this study. Even if ultrasonography had been performed, its diagnostic accuracy may have been limited by the chronicity of the condition, which could have resulted in subcutaneous tissue remodeling even in the absence of fibrosis. These considerations made advanced imaging techniques more appropriate for achieving diagnostic certainty in this case, as MRI has been shown to be particularly valuable for evaluating the vessels of the equine fetlock and foot [4].

In humans, for plantar venous thrombosis (PVT), the most prominent findings on magnetic resonance include intraluminal filling defects, perivenous edema and contrast enhancement, muscular edema, intravascular heterogeneous signal intensity, and venous ectasia extending through various muscle compartments along the course of the involved vein, with normal or enlarged caliber [1, 4]. In this study, the hyperintense T2‐weighted signal of a non‐pathologic vein was replaced by hypointense areas, a characteristic finding when a thrombus occludes a vein. The hypointensity affected no more than 40% of the lumen, and partial recanalization of the vessel was identified (hyperintense area in the remaining lumen), indicating healing and providing a more favorable prognosis. The moderate circumferential thickening of the soft tissues of the distal left hind limb was predominantly T2‐hyperintense, which is an indication of edema. These findings correspond to inflammatory soft tissue changes resulting from a combination of venous congestion and the inflammatory response to the thrombus.

The identification of a thrombus on MRI requires careful evaluation, as both normal digital veins and thrombi can have hyperintense signals. In normal veins, this signal is due to flow‐related phenomena, whereas in subacute thrombi it results from hemoglobin breakdown products (methemoglobin) and the absence of flow [10]. In this case, the thrombus had an approximately 4‐month history. Chronic thrombi often demonstrate heterogeneous signal intensity and may contain areas of hemosiderin deposition, causing susceptibility effects. Furthermore, at the presumed site of thrombosis, potential artifacts may simulate a filling defect, including partial volume averaging in small‐caliber vessels, position‐dependent venous stasis, signal loss or inhomogeneity caused by slow or turbulent venous flow, and local susceptibility effects from adjacent osseous and hoof structures [10]. The use of multiple MRI sequences is essential to accurately diagnose thrombosis. For this case, T2‐weighted and sPD sequences highlighted edema and soft tissue changes, whereas mDIXON and mDIXON FS sequences distinguished the thrombus from surrounding tissues and suppressed the fat signal. High‐resolution 3D VISTA sequences allowed multi‐plane reconstruction, facilitating a detailed evaluation of vessel morphology and assessment of partial recanalization. Finally, V3D SPIR sequences provided 3D fat‐suppressed imaging, improving the detection of subtle intraluminal thrombi. Although SPIR sequences generally suppress soft tissue fat effectively, medullary marrow fat was only partially suppressed in this case, a recognized limitation due to the short T1 relaxation time and heterogeneous composition of bone marrow. Importantly, this did not compromise the visualization of intraluminal thrombi.

In the reported case, the thrombus was identified as a fixed intraluminal structure with a hyperintense signal that persisted across different sequences and planes, contrasting with the dynamic signal expected from patent vessels. The persistent lesion, its separation from surrounding venous flow, and the associated clinical findings indicated thrombosis rather than artifact. Additionally, comparison with the contralateral limb helped confirm the diagnosis. This multi‐sequence approach allowed a confident diagnosis while minimizing ambiguity from flow‐related artifacts or anatomical variations.

Contrast‐enhanced MR venography may have provided useful information. Although it was not administered in this case, retrospective assessment suggested that non‐contrast sequences were sufficient to establish an accurate diagnosis, avoiding prolonged anesthesia. Prospective inclusion of contrast should be considered for similar cases to further enhance diagnostic certainty. This emphasizes the importance of tailoring MRI protocols for vascular lesions assessment in horses.

In equine patients, MRI system selection depends on clinical requirements, available resources, anesthesia considerations, and case complexity. Prior to admission, the left hind fetlock had been examined with MRI under general anesthesia at an outside institution, yielding an inconclusive diagnosis. That examination was performed using an open‐design low‐field system (0.25 T, 35.5 cm bore), and neither the images nor the protocol were available for review. Low‐field MRI systems offer advantages in accessibility and cost‐effectiveness but provide lower spatial resolution than high‐field systems and may be more susceptible to artifacts and geometric distortion, limiting evaluation of small or complex structures, and reducing diagnostic sensitivity in selected cases [13]. The discordant findings between the two studies are best understood in the context of disease chronicity and technical limitations. The suspected puncture wound occurred approximately 4 months before the low‐field examination, suggesting that the thrombosis had likely entered a chronic organized phase at the time of initial imaging, characterized by resolution of the T1 hyperintensity of subacute thrombus, replacement of perivenous edema by fibrosis, and potential partial recanalization, changes that are inherently subtle and less conspicuous than acute or subacute thrombosis on conventional sequences. These temporal factors were compounded by the small caliber of the lateral plantar digital vein and slice thicknesses of 2–4 mm typical of low‐field systems, resulting in partial volume averaging and reduced lesion conspicuity. The thin‐slice isotropic acquisitions, multiple fat‐suppressed sequences, and superior spatial resolution of the 3.0‐T system ultimately enabled the confident characterization of the chronic vascular changes, underscoring the diagnostic limitations of low‐field MRI for small vessel pathology in the equine distal limb.

Treatment of PVT has not been standardized in human literature [3, 6, 8]. Various therapies have demonstrated similar outcomes. Some studies suggest that non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) alone may be sufficient, whereas others advocate for a combination of anticoagulation therapy for 4–6 weeks and the use of elastic compression stockings or rest [2, 8]. Anticoagulation therapy is debated, given the potential for thrombus progression in the leg veins and documented risks of treatment‐related bleeding [3]. There is limited evidence on surgical treatments for this pathology in humans, but some reports described techniques such as catheter‐directed thrombolysis, inferior vena cava filter placement, and thrombus removal [14]. In this equine clinical case, anticoagulant therapy was not pursued due to limited evidence supporting its use in small‐caliber vessels in horses, the presence of partial recanalization on imaging, and the apparent stability of the thrombus. Instead, non‐medical treatment was implemented, including exercise recommendations and manual lymphatic drainage massage. It was hypothesized that, as the yearling matures, further collateral vessels and recanalization are expected to develop in the affected area, establishing an adequate blood supply, which should alleviate the edema and return the leg to normal size.

The outcomes reported in human literature are highly variable. In some cases, partial or complete recanalization of the affected vessel is observed after 6‐month follow‐up [8]. However, other reports describe a high recurrence rate (7%–23%), as well as sequelae (56%), residual pain, and slow recovery [6, 7]. As this lesion has not been previously described in horses, it is difficult to predict the outcome. Clinically, the follow‐up of the yearling shows improvements, with the swelling in the leg decreasing with exercise activity and no lameness, allowing the horse to train successfully. What has been described in human patients suggests that the leg swelling may not disappear, or may resolve very slowly. Assessing the evolution of the collateral vessels or recanalization of the reported case would require obtaining new images during future follow‐ups, which is a limitation of this study.

In conclusion, this case highlights a rare presentation of left lateral plantar digital vein thrombosis in a yearling, associated with secondary lymphatic dilation, limb edema, and partial recanalization of the affected vein. High‐field magnetic resonance was essential for a definitive diagnosis, providing a detailed visualization of the vein and surrounding tissues. This case report underscores the value of advanced imaging in evaluating complex vascular conditions in equine patients and demonstrates that, in the absence of significant complications, conservative management can yield favorable outcomes.

Outcomes and prognostic factors in dogs with subcutaneous and intramuscular hemangiosarcoma treated with hypofractionated radiation therapy and chemotherapy

## Ana Paula Rebelo *, Adriana Furtado , Rance Sellon , Gregory D. Roberts  and Janean Fidel

Department of Veterinary Clinical Sciences, College of Veterinary Medicine, Washington State University, Pullman, WA, United States

Introduction: Subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM) hemangiosarcoma (HSA) in dogs are aggressive malignancies with high rates of recurrence and metastasis. Surgery is the primary treatment, but incomplete excision is common, and the role of radiation therapy (RT) remains unclear. Methods: This single-institution retrospective study evaluated outcomes and tox­ icities in dogs with SC and IM HSA treated with hypofractionated RT using either 24 Gy in three 8-Gy fractions (days 0, 7, and 21) or 30 Gy in five 6-Gy fractions every other day, with or without surgery and chemotherapy. Results: Fifty-three dogs were included: 27/53 (51%) SC HSA and 26/53 (49%) IM HSA; 35/53 (66%) had macroscopic disease at RT. Overall, 47/53 (89%) received chemo­ therapy, of which 42/47 (89%) received doxorubicin; 35/42 (83%) received it concur­ rently with the first RT fraction. Among 30 evaluable dogs, the RT objective response rate (ORR) was 93% (37% complete, 56% partial). Local progression or recurrence (LPR) occurred in 11/36 (30%) dogs after a median of 128 days, predominantly with mac­ roscopic disease (10/11). Median time to progression (TTP) was not reached (95% CI, 621 days–not reached). In an exploratory multivariable Cox analysis, metastasis was associated with increased hazard of LPR (HR, 14.95; 95% CI, 2.84–78.72; p = 0.0014), whereas surgery was associated with a lower hazard, but not significantly (HR, 0.15; 95% CI, 0.018–1.24; p = 0.079). Overall median survival time (MST) was 306 days (95% CI, 284–875). On univariable analysis, anemia, absence of surgery, macroscopic dis­ ease at RT, metastasis, and tumor size at diagnosis >6 cm were associated with shorter survival. Dogs undergoing surgery prior to RT had longer survival (MST, 2059 vs. 287 days; p = 0.007). In multivariable analysis, anemia remained independently associated with increased hazard of death (HR, 3.20; 95% CI, 1.38–7.45; p = 0.0069), whereas metastasis, surgery, and tumor size were not independently associated with survival. Chemotherapy was not associated with survival. Radiation-associated adverse events were generally mild. Conclusion: Hypofractionated RT, as part of multimodal treatment in most dogs, was associated with a high ORR and may provide durable local control in dogs with non-visceral HSA.

## Introduction

Hemangiosarcoma (HSA), a highly aggressive malignant tumor of endothelial origin, is characterized by early and widespread metastasis (1, 2). In dogs, subcutaneous (SC) and intramuscular (IM) forms represent a clinically significant subset of cases (3). Surgical excision remains the primary treatment modality; however, due to the infiltrative nature of these tumors and their high risk of local recurrence, adjuvant therapies are frequently incorporated into treatment plans (4, 5). Among these, radiation therapy (RT) is com­ monly considered to improve local tumor control and potentially impact survival outcomes, although its definitive role in this setting remains uncertain (4–6).

The use of RT for microscopic disease following incomplete sur­ gical excision has been evaluated in a limited number of studies, which have been characterized by small sample sizes and inconsis­ tent results. In one retrospective analysis, dogs with SC and IM HSA treated with surgery and doxorubicin-based chemotherapy experi­ enced prolonged disease-free intervals (DFI) and median survival times (MST); however, a clear benefit of RT could not be demon­ strated (4). Notably, dogs with SC HSA that did not receive RT had significantly longer DFI (p < 0.001) and a trend toward longer MST (p = 0.052) compared with those that received RT. Additionally, among five dogs with incompletely excised tumors treated with definitive-course RT, local control was limited, with short response durations and three recurrences (4). In contrast, Shiu et al. reported no local recurrence in three dogs with incompletely resected tumors treated with RT, highlighting the variability in reported out­ comes (5).

Evidence supporting the use of RT in the gross disease setting is even more limited. Hillers et al. evaluated palliative RT in 20 dogs with non-splenic HSA using total doses ranging from 6 to 24 Gy and reported a 75% objective response rate (ORR) despite a short overall survival (95 days) in a heterogeneous population (6). Seventeen tumors involved soft tissues; however, the extent of invasion (e.g., SC or IM) could not be determined in many cases because most diagno­ ses were based on incisional biopsies. The remaining three tumors were located in the retroperitoneal space. Most dogs receiving 24 Gy were treated with 8 Gy × 3 fractions on days 0, 7, and 21, whereas three dogs received 6 Gy × 4 fractions on days 0, 7, 21, and 28 (6). McDonald et al. evaluated a 20-Gy palliative protocol delivered as 4 Gy × 5 consecutive daily fractions across multiple tumor types (7). The cohort included three dogs with macroscopic SC HSA, two of which demonstrated a reduction in tumor size, with response dura­ tions of 0.8 and 4.9 months; survival times for the three dogs were 1, 1.4, and 4.9 months (7).

Together, these studies provide limited but supportive evidence that hypofractionated RT can produce measurable tumor responses in dogs with macroscopic nonsplenic HSA. However, the small number of dogs with clearly characterized SC or IM HSA and the heterogeneity of the study populations, which included other non­ splenic presentations such as retroperitoneal HSA, limit conclusions regarding efficacy. Consequently, the contribution of RT specifically to outcomes in dogs with SC and IM HSA remains uncertain.

Overall, the current literature evaluating RT in dogs with SC and IM remains limited, with small cohorts, heterogeneous treatment pro­ tocols, and conflicting results, particularly with respect to its impact on local control and survival in both microscopic and macroscopic disease settings (1, 2, 4–7).

A hypofractionated protocol was selected because canine HSA is characterized by a high metastatic potential and poor long-term prog­ nosis (1, 2), making prolonged definitive-intent radiation protocols less attractive in many patients. In addition, as a mesenchymal tumor, HSA may share radiobiologic characteristics with other sarcomas, which are generally considered to have a relatively low α/β ratio (8). Tumors with a low α/β ratio are thought to derive greater biologic benefit from larger radiation doses per fraction, as higher fraction sizes are required to achieve an equivalent biologic effect compared with conventionally fractionated protocols (8). Therefore, treatment was primarily aimed at achieving local tumor control while minimiz­ ing treatment burden, reducing the number of anesthetic events, and allowing timely administration of systemic therapy.

The objectives of this study were to describe RT objective response rate (ORR), local progression or recurrence (LPR), time to progression (TTP), median survival time (MST), prognostic factors associated with LPR and survival, and treatment-related toxicities in dogs with SC and IM HSA treated with hypofractionated RT and chemotherapy.

## Materials and methods

This single-institution retrospective study included dogs that received hypofractionated RT for SC and IM HSA. The RT database was searched for all dogs with histologically or cytologically con­ firmed SC or IM HSA, with microscopic or macroscopic disease, with or without metastasis at initial evaluation that underwent hypofrac­ tionated RT between 2005 and 2023.

Data recorded included signalment (breed, age, sex, weight), clini­ cal signs, HSA locations as SC or IM, clinicopathological data, histo­ pathologic criteria including mitotic count and mitotic score (9), clinical stage, combination with surgery or chemotherapy before or after RT, RT protocol, RT and chemotherapy toxicities, LPR, and cause of death. All medical records were reviewed and supplemented, when necessary, by contacting referring veterinarians and/or owners to obtain updated information regarding disease status, recurrence, sur­ vival, and cause of death.

Computed tomography (CT) findings were reviewed when avail­ able and were used to determine tumor location. Hemangiosarcomas were categorized as SC or IM based on CT and/or histopathology assessment.

Histopathologic reports were reviewed when available. Mitotic figures were counted within an area of 2.37 mm2 and recorded as a continuous variable. In addition, tumors were assigned a mitotic score according to the grading scheme described by Moore et al. (9), with scores defined as 0 (0–10 mitoses/2.37 mm2), 1 (11–20 mito­ ses/2.37 mm2), 2 (21–30 mitoses/2.37 mm2), and 3 (>30 mito­ ses/2.37 mm2). These categories were used for subsequent statistical analyses.

Radiation therapy was delivered with a linear accelerator (Elekta SLi 15, Philips Medical Systems N.A., Bothell, WA, United States) using 6 MV photons or 8–12 MeV electron beams using a single field. All treatments were planned by the same board-certified radiation oncologist (JF) using manual or three-dimensional conformal RT (3D-CRT) radiation planning.

guide field design and dose distribution. In cases without a measurable gross tumor volume, treatment planning was based on the surgical scar and the estimated extent of microscopic disease. The extent of microscopic disease and treatment margins were determined by the treating radiation oncologist based on the expected biological behav­ ior and infiltrative nature of sarcomas, available histopathologic infor­ mation, tumor location, and anatomic constraints. Treatment margins were applied laterally and in depth, with adjustments based on ana­ tomic constraints and adjacent OARs. Treatment field margins were usually set at 3 cm from the tumor or surgical scar.

Field-shaping blocks (square and rectangular) were used for spe­ cific sizes in electron beam planning. Electron energy was selected based on lesion depth and proximity to organs at risk (OARs). Dose was prescribed to an appropriate isodose line according to electron depth dose tables generated for the linear accelerator by a medical physicist, to ensure target coverage. The prescribed isodose line ranged from 90% to 100% in this study. The planning goal was to cover at least 95% of the target volume with the prescribed dose.

For CT-based planning and treatment, patients were anesthetized and positioned in lateral or sternal recumbency (depending on the affected area) with stabilization provided by an individually moldable vacuum positioning mattress. Multiple vacuum positioning mattresses were used over the retrospective study period, and the specific manu­ facturer and model used for individual patients were not consistently documented. Dogs with tumors involving the head and neck were additionally positioned using a custom-made thermoplastic bite block fabricated in-house.

Pre- and post-contrast CT image sets were imported into the Prowess Panther Treatment Planning System version 5.01–5.1 (Prowess, Inc. 1844 Clayton Road, Concord, CA, 94520), depending on the year of treatment. Treatments were 3D-CRT plans. The gross tumor volume (GTV) was contoured to delineate visible macroscopic tumor on contrast-enhanced CT images. For macroscopic disease, the clinical target volume (CTV) encompassed the GTV plus a non-uni­ form margin for potential microscopic extension into surrounding tissues; margins were generally up to 3 cm in soft tissue such as muscle, but reduced when constrained by the skin surface, adjacent anatomy, or OAR. For postoperative microscopic disease, the CTV was based on the surgical scar/tumor bed and the estimated extent of microscopic disease, with margins similarly modified according to anatomic constraints. Regional lymph nodes were included only when clinically indicated. A uniform three-dimensional margin of 3 mm was added to the CTV to create the planning target volume (PTV), accounting for internal motion, patient movement, and setup uncer­ tainty. Planning objectives included 99% of the GTV (D99) and 95% of the PTV (D95) receiving 100% of the prescribed total dose.

Kilovoltage port films were used at each treatment to ensure accu­ rate tumor positioning. Digital films (Fujifilm type IP cassette, Fuji Photofilm Co. LTD, Tokyo, Japan) were used for larger fields and improved tissue discrimination than onboard imaging and were reviewed by one author (JF).

Two hypofractionated radiation protocols were employed: a total prescribed dose of 24 Gy delivered in three 8-Gy fractions on days 0, 7, and 21, or a total prescribed dose of 30 Gy delivered in five 6-Gy fractions administered every other day. Selection of the protocol was based on the feasibility of coordinating doxorubicin administration with RT treatments (most practical with the 8 Gy × 3 fraction proto­ col, in which doxorubicin was administered on days 0 and 21), logisti­ cal considerations including owner ability to travel for multiple

outpatient visits versus short-term hospitalization for the every-otherday 6 Gy × 5 fraction protocol, and financial factors, as the threefraction protocol was more cost-effective and required fewer anesthetic events. Although the fractionation schedules differed, the protocols were selected to provide a comparable biologically effective dose (BED), thereby maintaining a broadly similar modeled biological effect while allowing flexibility in treatment planning and patient management. BED calculations based on the linear-quadratic model do not account for the different overall treatment times of these pro­ tocols (days 0, 7, and 21 for 8 Gy × 3 versus approximately 9 days for 6 Gy × 5); therefore, BED comparison alone may not fully capture dif­ ferences in tumor repopulation or normal-tissue effects between schedules.

Local progression was defined as an increase in size of a treated macroscopic tumor following an initial response to therapy, whereas recurrence was defined as the reappearance of a previously surgically removed tumor after a documented period of no evidence of disease following adjuvant RT. For subsequent analyses, local progression and local recurrence were combined into a single outcome, herein referred to as local progression or recurrence (LPR), rather than evaluated independently. Tumor size was categorized as ≤ 4 cm, 4–6 cm, and > 6 cm for statistical analysis, consistent with the categories used by Shiu et al. (5).

Tumor response to RT was assessed retrospectively according to the Veterinary Cooperative Oncology Group Response Evaluation Criteria for Solid Tumors in Dogs (VCOG RECIST v1.0) (10). Response was classified as complete response (CR) defined as disap­ pearance of all target lesions; partial response (PR) defined as ≥ 30% decrease in the sum of the diameters of target lesions; progressive dis­ ease (PD) defined as ≥ 20% increase in the sum of diameters of target lesions, or the appearance of new lesions; and stable disease (SD) defined as <30% reduction or <20% increase in the sum of diameters of target lesions (10).

Tumor response and LPR were assessed retrospectively from available medical records. When recorded, measurable superficial lesions were assessed by physical examination with caliper measure­ ments; cross-sectional imaging was reviewed when it had been per­ formed for clinical reassessment. Systemic progression was assessed using the restaging studies available for each dog, which could include thoracic radiographs or thoracic CT, abdominal ultrasonography, and other clinically indicated imaging. Response and progression assess­ ments were based on the best available documentation for each patient. The institutional recommendation was for patients to undergo a post-treatment recheck approximately 3–4 weeks after completion of RT to assess resolution of acute treatment-related adverse effects and evaluate the treated tumor site. This initial recheck could be per­ formed at the referring veterinarian (rDVM). Thereafter, surveillance was recommended every 3–4 months and generally included a physi­ cal examination to assess for LPR, thoracic radiographs, possible abdominal ultrasound, and imaging of the treated tumor site when clinically indicated. Follow-up could be performed either at our insti­ tution or by the rDVM, depending on logistical considerations and owner preference.

Radiation therapy-associated adverse events were retrospectively graded according to the Veterinary Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (VRTOG) v2.0 criteria (11). Acute adverse events were defined as those occurring during or within 3 months after completion of RT, whereas late adverse events were defined as those arising or persisting more than 3 months after completion of RT (11). ## Results

Fifty-three dogs with cytologically or histopathologically con­ firmed SC and IM HSA were included in the study.

## Signalment

The median age was 10 years (range, 4–14 years) and the median weight was 28.5 kg (range 7.3–76.6 kg). There were 24 spayed females and 29 males (28 neutered). The most common pure breeds were Labrador Retriever (8), Golden Retriever (4), Miniature Schnauzer (3), German Shepherd (2), Whippet (2), Australian Shepherd (2), Border Collie (2), Cairn Terrier (2) and 1 each of 14 additional purebreed dogs; 14 dogs were mixed breed.

## Clinical signs, HSA location and stage

Hemangiosarcomas were categorized as SC or IM based upon CT imaging and histopathology when available. Twenty-seven dogs (51%) were diagnosed with SC HSA and 26 dogs (49%) with IM HSA. All dogs had clinical signs, including mass effect (50), pain (9), lameness (8), bleeding/ulceration (5), swelling (3), lethargy (3), drooling/dys­ phagia (2), and dyspnea (1).

Tumor anatomic sites included pelvic limb (13/53, 24%), head (11/53 20%), inguinal region (8/53, 15%), thoracic limb (7/53, 13%),

epaxial musculature (4/53, 8%), neck (4/53, 8%), axilla (3/53, 6%), abdominal wall/flank (2/53, 4%), and perineal region (1/53, 2%).

Staging tests performed were variable between dogs. Complete blood count and serum biochemistry panel results were available at diagnosis for all 53 dogs. Anemia was identified in 11 dogs (21%) and thrombocytopenia in 10 dogs (19%), based on the reference intervals of the reporting laboratories. No consistent abnormalities were noted on serum biochemical analysis.

Fifty-two of 53 dogs (98%) had thoracic radiographs or computed tomography and abdominal ultrasound performed at or around the time of diagnosis; pulmonary nodules consistent with metastatic dis­ ease were identified in 14 dogs (27%) and intraabdominal metastasis confirmed via cytology in 4 dogs (8%). Forty-six dogs (87%) had echocardiogram and 2 dogs (5%) had right auricle masses. Staging in one dog consisted only of a complete blood count and serum bio­ chemistry panel, with no diagnostic imaging performed. The overall known metastatic rate at the time of diagnosis was 38% (20/52).

## Tumor identification and treatments

Five dogs (9%) had a cytological diagnosis, and 48 dogs (91%) had a histopathological diagnosis. All cytologic evaluations were per­ formed by board-certified clinical pathologists and were consistent with sarcoma with features suggestive of HSA. Mitotic count was available in 37 cases, with a median of 11 mitotic figures per 2.37 mm2 (range 0–80). Dogs with microscopic disease at RT time had a lower median mitotic count (7; range, 1–40) compared with those with mac­ roscopic disease (12; range, 0–80). Based on mitotic figures per 2.37 mm2, mitotic scores were: 0 (0–10; n = 18), 1 (11–20; n = 7), 2 (21–30; n = 7), and 3 (>30; n = 5).

Tumor size at diagnosis was available for 50 dogs: 16 (≤4 cm), 10 (>4 cm and ≤6 cm), and 24 (>6 cm) (Table 1). At RT time, 35 (66%) had macroscopic disease, 4 (≤4 cm), 7 (>4 cm and ≤6 cm), and 21(>6 cm); median tumor size was >6 cm. Three cases lacked measur­ able size (multiple masses, no measurement, or non-measurable facial swelling). Eighteen dogs (34%) had surgery prior to RT; margins were dirty (9/18, 50%), narrow (7/18, 38%), complete (1/18, 6%), and unavailable (1/18, 6%), with a median tumor size <4 cm.

## Radiation therapy

Of the 53 dogs, 24 (45%) had manual planning and were treated with a single electron beam field (8–12 MeV) and 29 (55%) had 3D-CRT delivered via 6 MV photons with either a single beam or parallel opposed beams. The regional lymph node was only irradiated in one patient. Regarding RT protocols, 83% (44/53) received 8 Gy × 3 fractions (total dose 24 Gy), and 17% (9/53) received 6 Gy × 5 frac­ tions (total dose of 30 Gy). Three dogs underwent re-irradiation at 91, 489, and 706 days following the initial treatment; the first was treated with electrons and the latter two with photons.

## Chemotherapy

Forty-seven dogs (89%) received chemotherapy, of which 42 (89%) received doxorubicin with a median of 3 doses (1–6 doses). The starting doxorubicin dosage was 30 mg/m2 (n = 33) or 1 mg/kg if <15 kg (n = 5); 3 dogs received lower doses (15–25 mg/m2), and dosage was unrecorded in 1. Dose adjustments were at clinician dis­ cretion. Thirty-five dogs (83%) received doxorubicin on the same day as the first RT dose, 4 (10%) before RT, and 1 (2%) after RT comple­ tion; timing was not recorded in 2 (5%). Five of 47 dogs (10%) received metronomic lomustine (2.87 mg/m2 orally once daily): 1 before RT, 2 after RT completion, and 2 with unknown timing.

After completion of the RT and doxorubicin, 15 dogs received additional chemotherapy. Thirteen received metronomic chemother­ apy, including lomustine (7), cyclophosphamide (4), and chlorambucil (2). One dog received a single lomustine dose (54 mg/m2), and one received toceranib (unknown dosage).

## Chemotherapy-related toxicosis

Episodes of toxicosis were recorded 50 times among 31 dogs receiving chemotherapy, with 30 of those dogs experiencing events associated with doxorubicin (Table 2). No adverse effects were reported in 9 dogs, and toxicity data were unavailable for 7 dogs. Eight dogs required doxorubicin dose reductions due to toxicosis: grade 1 neutropenia (1), grade 1 neutropenia and gastrointestinal side effects (1), grade 3 neutropenia (1), grade 4 neutropenia (3), and neutropenia of unspecified grade (2). The only toxicity observed with metronomic lomustine was hepatotoxicity in one dog; data were unavailable for the remaining four.

## Outcome

Five dogs were lost to follow-up, and three were still alive at the time of data compilation. Median follow-up time was 1,346 days (range, 134–2,136 days).

Of the 35 dogs with macroscopic disease that underwent RT, 30 had response data; 28 (93%) achieved an objective response, including 11 (37%) CR and 17 (56%) PR.

Among these 30 dogs, 22 received doxorubicin concurrently with RT; 21/22 achieved an objective response (10 CR and 11 PR), while one had SD. Four dogs had received doxorubicin before RT and had either failed to respond or were no longer responding to doxorubicin when RT was initiated; all four subsequently achieved an objective response following RT (three PR and one CR). One additional dog had a PR documented at the time metronomic lomustine was initiated one week after completion of RT, and another dog had a PR documented at the time doxorubicin was initiated after completion of RT. In two dogs, the timing of chemotherapy relative to RT could not be reliably determined from the medical records. Dates of initial and maximal tumor response were not consistently documented; therefore, time to response and the association between concurrent doxorubicin admin­ istration and response timing could not be reliably evaluated.

Local progression or recurrence data were available for 36/53 dogs, of which 11 (30%) experienced LPR after a median of 128 days (range, 44–1,675 days); median TTP was not reached (95% CI: 621 days–not reached). Most events occurred in dogs with macro­ scopic disease at RT time (10/11), including 5 PR, 3 CR, and 2 SD (median mitotic count was 24; mitotic score 2). Out of the animals with microscopic disease, only one recurrence occurred in a dog with microscopic disease following surgery (<4 cm SC HSA on the thoracic limb, dirty margins, mitotic count 1; mitotic score 0), 317 days after RT. Among dogs categorized by best response, median TTP was not reached for dogs achieving CR (95% CI, 180 days–NR), 397 days for dogs achieving PR (95% CI, 114 days–NR), and 906 days for dogs with SD (95% CI, 138 days–NR); response category was not significantly associated with LPR (p = 0.43).

Margin status was available in 17/18 dogs undergoing surgery prior to RT. Among 12 with known recurrence status, no LPR occurred with clean (n = 1) or narrow margins (n = 5), while 1/6 (17%) with dirty margins developed LPR.

Use of chemotherapy was not associated with LPR (p = 0.29). Among six dogs without chemotherapy, five had prior surgery (mar­ gins: two narrow, two dirty) with no recurrences, while one dog with gross disease (SD) developed LPR at 138 days post-RT.

Among dogs with evaluable LPR data, several clinicopathologic variables were significantly associated with TTP (Table 3). Surgery prior to RT significantly improved local control (p = 0.0079), with median TTP not reached versus 621 days (95% CI: 173–NR) with RT alone. Tumor size at diagnosis was strongly prognostic (p = 0.0038), with tumors >6 cm having shorter TTP (173 days, 95% CI: 119–NR), versus not reached for tumors ≤6 cm. Similarly, anemia at diagnosis was associated with significantly shorter TTP (median 173 days, 95% CI: 119–NR vs. not reached; p = 0.0023). Higher mitotic score was also associated with worse local control (p = 0.028), with score 3 tumors experiencing rapid progression (median 56 days, 95% CI: 44–NR), while lower scores had prolonged disease control. Metastasis at diag­ nosis was a strong negative prognostic factor (p < 0.0001), with a median TTP 119 days (95% CI: 114–NR) compared to not reached in dogs without metastasis.

In contrast, HSA location was not significantly associated with LPR (p = 0.90), with a median TTP of not reached (NR; 95% CI, 621 days–NR) for IM HSA and 1,675 days (95% CI, 317 days–NR) for SC HSA. Similarly, thrombocytopenia was not associated with LPR (p = 0.29), with a median TTP of NR (95% CI, 621 days–NR) in dogs without thrombocytopenia and NR (95% CI, 119 days–NR) in dogs with thrombocytopenia. No significant difference was observed between RT protocols (p = 0.28); dogs treated with 8 Gy × 3 fractions had a median TTP of NR (95% CI, 1,675 days–NR), whereas dogs treated with 6 Gy × 5 fractions had a median TTP of 621 days (95% CI, 173 days–NR). Likewise, response to RT was not significantly associated with LPR (p = 0.43), with median TTPs of NR (95% CI, 180 days–NR), 397 days (95% CI, 114 days–NR), and 906 days (95% CI, 138 days–NR) for dogs achieving CR, PR, and SD, respectively.

In univariable Cox proportional hazards analysis for time to LPR, tumor size > 6 cm (HR, 15.69; 95% CI, 1.10–223.8; p = 0.042) and the presence of metastatic disease at diagnosis (HR, 28.1; 95% CI, 2.99– 264.24; p = 0.0035) were significantly associated with an increased risk of LPR. However, the effect of metastasis was associated with model instability, likely due to separation, and should be interpreted with caution. Surgery prior to RT (HR, 0.15; 95% CI, 0.02–1.25; p = 0.079), gross disease at the time of RT (HR, 6.83; 95% CI, 0.79–59.2; p = 0.079), and increasing mitotic score (HR, 1.74; 95% CI, 0.92–3.32; p = 0.091) demonstrated trends toward association with LPR but did not reach statistical significance. Although anemia was associated with shorter TTP in Kaplan–Meier analysis, it was not significantly associ­ ated with LPR in univariable Cox regression (HR, 5.43; 95% CI, 0.55– 53.11; p = 0.146). Thrombocytopenia and tumor location were not significantly associated with TTP.

Thrombocytopenia and mitotic score showed trends toward an asso­ ciation with overall survival but did not reach statistical significance. Tumor location (SC vs. IM) was not significantly associated with survival.

Variables considered clinically relevant based on previous studies and biologic plausibility were subsequently included in a multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis for survival (Table 5). The final model included 37 dogs, with 24 events recorded. Anemia at the time of diagnosis remained independently associated with decreased overall survival (HR, 3.20; 95% CI, 1.38–7.45; p = 0.0069). Metastasis (HR, 1.81; 95% CI, 0.70–4.66; p = 0.220) and surgery (HR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.20–1.69; p = 0.319) were not independently associated with overall survival. Gross disease, thrombocytopenia, tumor extension, and mitotic score were not independently associated with survival after adjustment for the other variables.

Cause of death was available for 35 dogs. Eight dogs (23%) were euthanized for causes unrelated to HSA, including poor mobility (2 dogs), age-related causes of unspecified reason (2 dogs), trauma, acute leukemia, primary pulmonary carcinoma (lungs were not in the RT field; no evidence of HSA at necropsy), and laryngeal paraly­ sis (pre-existing chronic condition; potential contribution of anes­ thesia cannot be excluded, as death occurred 8 days following the

final RT treatment in a reirradiation case; the radiation field did not include the head or neck). The remaining 27 dogs (77%) were eutha­ nized due to disease progression, unknown causes, or were found deceased and were therefore classified as tumor-related deaths.

## Discussion

To the authors’ knowledge, this study represents the first and largest cohort dedicated exclusively to dogs with SC and IM HSA treated with RT, avoiding the heterogeneity introduced by inclusion of other nonsplenic HSA subtypes reported in previous studies. The results demonstrate that hypofractionated RT, delivered in conjunc­ tion with chemotherapy in most dogs, provides clinically meaning­ ful disease control. The ORR of 93% observed in dogs with measurable disease is comparable to the approximately 75% ORR reported by Hillers et al. (6) and McDonald et al. (7) in dogs with nonsplenic HSA treated with a similar hypofractionated radiation protocol. In addition, complete responses were observed in 37% of dogs in the present study, compared with 20% in the Hillers cohort. These findings support the reproducibility of hypofractionated RT as an effective local treatment strategy for gross HSA. While direct comparison between studies should be interpreted cautiously because Hillers et al. included a more heterogeneous population of nonsplenic HSA, including retroperitoneal tumors, the consistency of response rates across studies suggests meaningful response of this tumor type. Importantly, dogs with macroscopic disease at the time of RT achieving complete or partial responses frequently maintained local tumor control for prolonged periods, with a median TTP of 397 days among dogs achieving a PR and median TTP not reached among dogs achieving a CR. Although response category was not significantly associated with TTP in the present study, these findings suggest that hypofractionated RT can provide durable local disease control in a subset of patients. Nevertheless, LPR occurred in 30% of evaluable dogs, indicating that despite excellent initial response rates, durable local control remains a therapeutic challenge.

The present findings also provide insight into the potential role of RT for microscopic disease following surgery. Of the 11 LPR events observed, 10 occurred in dogs treated for gross dis­ ease, whereas only one event was documented in a dog treated with surgery followed by adjuvant RT for microscopic disease. These findings suggest that hypofractionated RT may provide adequate local control of microscopic residual disease. The use of RT for microscopic residual disease following incomplete surgical excision has been investigated in a limited number of studies, with conflicting results regarding its impact on local recurrence and survival. In the study by Bulakowski et al., five dogs received definitive-intent RT after incomplete excision; however, RT was not associated with improved disease-free interval or survival, and three of the four evaluable dogs developed local recurrence (4). Comparison with the present study is challenging because sub­ stantially different radiation protocols were employed. Whereas Bulakowski et al. primarily used conventionally fractionated definitive-intent RT protocols, all dogs in the present study received hypofractionated RT, which may produce different radio­ biologic effects in sarcomas. Although margin status was available for only a subset of dogs, the low rate of LPR among dogs with known incomplete or narrow margins suggests that hypofractionated RT combined with chemo­ therapy may provide effective control of microscopic residual dis­ ease. microscopic disease, larger studies with more complete surgical margin assessment are needed to better define its impact on local tumor control.

Metastatic disease, larger tumor size, and anemia were associ­ ated with worse outcomes, consistent with prior reports and their potential role as markers of greater disease burden (1, 2, 4, 6, 7). Although metastasis and tumor size were not independently associ­ ated with survival after multivariable adjustment, metastasis remained associated with increased risk of LPR, while anemia remained independently associated with decreased survival. The higher prevalence of anemia among dogs with metastatic disease further suggests that anemia may serve as a surrogate marker of advanced disease.

Intramuscular involvement was not associated with survival in the present study, consistent with the findings of Shiu et al. (5), suggesting that disease burden and adequacy of local control may be more important determinants of outcome than anatomic loca­ tion alone. In contrast, Bulakowski et al. (4) reported shorter sur­ vival times for dogs with IM tumors. One possible explanation for this discrepancy is that IM tumors may be detected later in their clinical course because they are less readily visible or palpable than SC masses, potentially resulting in larger tumor size, more extensive local invasion, or a greater likelihood of occult meta­ static disease at the time of diagnosis. Given that tumor size has been identified as a prognostic factor in both the present study and previous reports, the apparent effect of tumor location observed in some studies may partially reflect differences in dis­ ease burden rather than location itself. However, the retrospective nature of available studies and the relatively small number of IM tumors evaluated preclude definitive conclusions regarding the prognostic significance of tumor location.

The relationship between initial tumor response and long-term local control should also be interpreted cautiously. Response to RT was not significantly associated with LPR or survival, indicating that early tumor shrinkage may not necessarily predict long-term out­ come, consistent with the findings of Hillers et al. (6). Although dogs achieving CR or PR frequently experienced prolonged local control, these findings emphasize the distinction between objective tumor response and durable disease control. Nevertheless, the high ORR observed in dogs with macroscopic disease supports consideration of hypofractionated RT as a palliative or cytoreductive treatment option when surgery is not feasible or in advanced disease.

No significant differences in outcome were detected between the two hypofractionated RT protocols; however, interpretation is limited by the small number of dogs treated with 6 Gy × 5 fractions. These findings are consistent with those reported by Hillers et al. (6), in which hypofractionated RT achieved high objective response rates in dogs with gross nonsplenic HSA. Taken together, the results of both studies support the use of hypofractionated RT as an effective approach for local control of gross disease, while offering the practical advantages of shorter treatment duration and reduced treatment burden compared with definitive protocols.

Three dogs underwent re-irradiation months to years after initial treatment, suggesting that repeat RT may be feasible in select cases. Although outcomes could not be formally assessed, this observation raises the possibility that local recurrence may be amenable to salvage therapy when surgical excision is not feasible. Prospective studies are needed to better define cumulative dose constraints, toxicity profiles, and the clinical benefit of re-irradiation.

Chemotherapy was not associated with LPR or survival in the present study; however, interpretation of its efficacy is limited by the high rate of chemotherapy use, lack of a standardized treatment pro­ tocol, small number of dogs not receiving chemotherapy, and absence of a control group. While most dogs received doxorubicin concur­ rently with RT, any potential radiosensitizing effect remains specula­ tive. However, objective responses were also observed in dogs that were not receiving doxorubicin concurrently with RT. Notably, four dogs had received doxorubicin before RT and had either failed to respond or were no longer responding when RT was initiated; all four subsequently achieved an objective response following RT. This obser­ vation supports a contribution of RT to tumor response in these dogs, although the small number of cases and retrospective study design preclude conclusions regarding the independent effect of RT or a potential interaction between RT and chemotherapy. Because response assessments were not performed at standardized time points, the influence of concurrent doxorubicin on response timing could not be reliably evaluated.

Importantly, the combination was generally well tolerated, with most radiation-associated adverse events being mild and the only grade 4 toxicity having no documented adverse impact on the patient’s quality of life. Chemotherapy-associated toxicities were generally manageable, supporting the tolerability of this multimodal treatment approach. Although a survival benefit of chemotherapy could not be demonstrated in this study, doxorubicin-based protocols have been associated with improved outcomes in dogs with visceral HSA, par­ ticularly splenic HSA, and remain a cornerstone of treatment because of the high metastatic potential of this disease (13–15). Therefore, the lack of a detectable effect in the present study should not be inter­ preted as evidence of a lack of benefit, but rather as a reflection of study design and limited ability to independently evaluate chemo­ therapy efficacy.

Limitations of this study include its retrospective design, variabil­ ity in treatment selection, and inherent selection bias. In addition, several clinical and disease characteristics included in the multivari­ able analyses were likely interrelated. For example, dogs with larger tumors, macroscopic disease, or metastatic disease may have been less likely to undergo surgery, resulting in potential confounding among tumor burden, disease stage, and treatment selection. Consequently, the absence of an independent association for variables such as sur­ gery, tumor size, and metastasis after multivariable adjustment should not be interpreted as evidence that these factors are not clinically rel­ evant. Rather, their individual effects may be difficult to distinguish in this retrospective cohort, particularly given the limited number of events and relatively small sample size. Although the two hypofrac­ tionated protocols had broadly comparable calculated BED values, BED does not account for differences in overall treatment time. The 8 Gy × 3 protocol was delivered over 21 days, whereas the 6 Gy × 5 protocol was delivered every other day over a substantially shorter interval; therefore, potential differences in tumor repopulation and time-dependent normal-tissue effects are not reflected by BED com­ parison alone. Tumor response and progression were also assessed retrospectively and at non-standardized time points, primarily through serial clinical examinations and measurements rather than uniform cross-sectional imaging. Consequently, RECIST classification may have been less precise, particularly for small or deep changes in tumor dimensions, and time to initial and maximal response could not be reliably determined. Finally, missing data reduced cases

available for multivariable analysis, and non-standardized manage­ ment at progression may have influenced survival outcomes.

In conclusion, hypofractionated RT was associated with a high ORR and may provide durable local control in dogs with SC and IM HSA. LPR occurred predominantly in dogs treated for macro­ scopic disease, whereas recurrence was uncommon following sur­ gery and RT for microscopic disease. Surgery was associated with improved local control and survival in unadjusted analyses, although potential selection bias should be considered. Metastatic disease and tumor size were associated with adverse outcomes, while anemia remained independently associated with decreased survival and metastasis with increased hazard of LPR in multivari­ able analyses. Taken together, the present findings suggest that hypofractionated RT may have a role in managing microscopic disease following surgery; however, the small number of dogs in this subgroup and potential differences in disease characteristics and treatment selection limit definitive conclusions regarding its benefit.

These findings support further investigation of multimodal treatment strategies incorporating surgery, hypofractionated RT, and systemic therapy. Prospective studies, ideally including dogs with more consistent disease characteristics and stage, are war­ ranted to better define and confirm the potential benefit of hypo­ fractionated RT in the early-stage or microscopic disease setting, as well as to further characterize prognostic factors for local con­ trol and survival.

Active metasurfaces provide the opportunity for fast spatio-temporal control of light. Among various tuning methods, organic electro-optic materials provide some unique advantages due to their fast speed and large nonlinearity, along with the possibility of using fabrication techniques based on inﬁltration. In this letter, we report a silicon-organic platform where organic electro-optic material is inﬁltrated into the narrow gaps of slot-mode metasurfaces with high quality factors. The mode conﬁnement into the slot enables the placement of metallic electrodes in close proximity, thus enabling tunability at lower voltages. We demonstrate the maximum tuning sensitivity of 0.16nm/V, the maximum extinction ratio of 38% within ± 17V voltage at telecommunication wavelength. The device has 3dB bandwidth of 3MHz. These results provide a path towards tunable silicon-organic hybrid metasurfaces at CMOS-level voltages.

Relying on sub-wavelength nanostructures, metasurfaces have been shown as promising candidates for replacing conventional free-space optical components by arbitrarily manipulating the amplitude, phase, and polarization of optical wavefronts in certain applications1–3. In recent years, the scope of their applications has been expanded towards complete spatio-temporal control through the introduction of active metasurfaces. These developments open up exciting new possibilities for dynamic holography4, faster spatial light modulators5, and fast optical beam steering for LiDAR6. Large efforts have been channeled into various modulation mechanisms7. Microelectromechanical and nanoelectromechanical systems (MEMS and NEMS)8–11 have the advantages of low-cost and CMOS-compatibility, but the speed is limited up to MHz. Phase-change materials12–14 have fast, drastic, and non-volatile refractive index change, but lack continuous refractive index tuning and have a limited number of cycles constraining applicability to reconﬁgurable devices. Through molecule reorientation, liquid crystal can have index modulation over 10%, while under relatively low applied voltages Tunable liquid crystal

metasurfaces, U.S. patent number 10,665,953 [Application Number 16/505,687]15. Techniques of liquid crystal integration have also advanced after decades of development. However, the tuning speeds are limited to kHz range16. Thermal-optic effects can induce relatively large refractive index changes17,18, but the speed is inherently limited and the on-chip thermal management can be challenging. The cointegration of transparent conductive oxide and metallic plasmonic structures5,6 has been demonstrated in epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) regime to control the wavefront of reﬂected light, but the low reﬂection amplitude induced by the optical loss of the materials and the ENZ regime is unavoidable. As a result, under the same bias voltage, the slot mode has the largest resonance shift, as demonstrated through the simulation results in Fig. 2g–i. With the same amount of index change in the active region, Mode I, II, and III have resonance shifts of 2.73nm, 0.29nm, and 0.46nm, respectively. A more accurate model estimates the overlap factor by considering the orientation of the nonlinearity29 (see supplementary material section 2). The calculated Γ based on this model for modes I, II, and III are 0.156, 0.017, and 0.015, respectively. The slot mode shows an order of magnitude higher Γc, compared to the others. Therefore, the slot mode is crucial for lowvoltage modulation in silicon-organic metasurfaces. We experimentally realize the concept discussed above, using a silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer. The device’s cross-section, top view, and voltage setting are schematically illustrated in Fig. 3a, b. The detailed device parameters are shown in supplementary material section 7. The nanostructures are fabricated with conventional nanofabrication techniques (see Methods section for details on the fabrication procedure). The step-by-step zoom-out scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images (prior to spin-coating of the OEO material) are shown in Fig. 3c–f. Doped silicon nano-bars have a resistance of 1 ~ 10Ω ⋅cm, and ~100nm wide gold strips along the nano-bars are added to further reduce the voltage drop across the silicon. In Fig. 3c, the gold strips are deliberately aligned at the center of the silicon rail so that only minimal absorption is introduced (See supplementary section 3 and Fig. S3). Figure 3e shows an 80 × 100 μm2 device. Multiple devices are fabricated on a chip as shown in Fig. 3f for increasing

To experimentally verify the relationship between resonant optical characteristics of the slot modes and the geometry of the device, we fabricated several devices having different design parameters and compared their measured optical properties with corresponding numerical calculations (see methods, supplementary section 6, and Fig. S7 for details in optical measurement setup). Figure 4 shows the calculated and measured spectra of the slot mode resonances with different geometries. We characterize the slot resonances by varying the notch period and notch size in Fig. 4a, b and c, d, respectively. In Fig. 4a, b, we observe that a 20 nm increment in notch periodicity leads to ~21.6 nm and 22.2 nm average redshift of the resonance in simulation and experiment, respectively. Also, with respect to the resonant wavelengths, the resonance amplitudes, and the spectral shapes of the resonance, the measured spectra in Fig. 4c show good agreement with the calculated spectra in Fig. 4d. In particular, the quality factor increases with the decrease of the resonance amplitude. This trade-off is mainly due to the decreasing radiation rate to the top port (to +z direction), which results in the under-coupling between the slot mode and the illuminated light from the top18. Speciﬁcally, the amplitude of the resonance is determined by the ratio of the mode coupling rate between the input light and the slot mode to the sum of other undesired decay rates43. The undesired decays include absorption in the gold layer, scattering from the rough sidewalls or ﬁnite edges of the chip, and radiation to the oxide layer or the silicon substrate. As the absorption in the gold layer and the radiation to the silicon substrate are nearly inevitable in the proposed planar structures, the trade-off between the resonance amplitude and the quality factor is inevitable, especially when the coupling rate decreases. The proposed devices in Fig. 4e can achieve modulation amplitude over 10% and Q-factor over 1000 in the experiment even with the absorption in the gold. Operation results under DC bias are shown in Fig. 5. Figure 5a–c show the results from 3 different devices under maximum bias voltages before any dielectric breakdown. In Fig. 5e, the relative modulation ratio, ΔR/R, from the device in Fig. 5c is plotted. The maximum modulation ratio is over 40%. It is worth noting that the asymmetry of the modulation is due to the Fano shape of the resonance45. The model collectively considers the contributing factors to the response speed within and outside the devices. In the devices, we model the nano-bars as a resistance, including the contribution from the gold strip RAu and the silicon nano-bar RSi (see supplementary section 4). Discussion In this work, we propose a silicon-organic metasurface for free-space modulation with reduced operation voltage less than ± 17V. We experimentally observed the resonance with quality factor 330–1310 and up to ~5.5nm shift with nonlinear coefﬁcient r33 = 45.7pm/V at 1495 nm. The proposed slot mode combines the advantages of a short distance between two electrodes and a large overlap with the OEO material, achieving a tuning sensitivity Sabs = 0.161nm/V, which shows an improvement with a factor of 1.6 in sensitivity compared to the state-of-art31,44. Finally, the metasurface has up to 3MHz bandwidth. The use of the slot mode is not limited to electro-optic systems. The proposed design approach can be applied to any system where sensitivity to perturbations in low-index media is critical. For example, in

The currently demonstrated sensitivity is limited by the quality factor and the nonlinear coefﬁcient r33. The quality factor could be improved by using smaller notches or a reﬁned fabrication process. The relatively low nonlinear coefﬁcient compared to what we expected27 is partly due to the surface state of doped silicon used as the electrode52 and the small width of the slot41. Barrier layer protection53 has the potential to increase the nonlinear coefﬁcient r33 by 4-5 times54, reducing the tuning voltage down to CMOS-level. Judicious doping level adjustments and the microwave coplanar waveguide design could enable GHz speed operation31,36. Therefore, with the increase of electro-optic coefﬁcient and operation bandwidth, our platform is a potential solution for GHz free-space modulation at the CMOS level voltage. This study primarily focuses on structures which are periodic in both x and y dimensions. However, it is not a necessary condition for preserving the slot mode. As a mode propagating along the y direction, the slot mode doesn’t necessitate periodic conditions in x direction55. By varying the geometry of the slots, individual slot modulation could be potentially achieved. In the y-dimension, by introducing high contrast index variations or photonic crystal mirrors, the footprint of the resonant device could be reduced considerably56,57. Furthermore, the

proposed devices expect to achieve phase modulation if the overcoupling condition is satisﬁed by the out-of-plane asymmetry in nanostructures10 or a bottom mirror5,6. In summary, this report presents a low-voltage amplitude modulator using a silicon-organic platform. The slot mode metasurface has the potential to enable high-speed and low-voltage optical switching, sensing, and tuning, for numerous applications such as LiFi, LiDAR, spatial light modulators, and quantum optical communication.
